# Introduction

## Introduction

- an alternative method for selecting a sample with equal selection probabilities
- offers practical advantages
    1. in situ (i.e. sample selection can be carried out in the field)
    2. easy to implement

## Introduction

::: {.block}
::: {.block-title}
Idea
:::
one individual is selected at random among the first $G$ individuals of the list (frame).
:::

- $G=$ sampling interval
- $G$ is an integer and chosen in advance

The rest of the sample is determined by systematically choosing every $G$-th individual.

There are only $G$ distinct/possible samples, i.e. $p(s)=G^{-1}$.

## Definition

Let $G=N/n$ be the sampling interval and $n$ the integer part of $N/G$:

$$N=nG+c$$

where $0\leq c \leq G$.

The sample size can be $n$ or $n+1$.

## Selection method

As a first step, we select an integer among $\{1,2,\dots,G\}$.

If $r$ (any individual) is selected, then:

$$
  s_r =
    \begin{cases}
      \{ r, r+G, r+2G,\dots,r+(n-1)G \} & \text{if } c<r \leq G\\
      \{ r, r+G, r+2G,\dots,r+nG \} & \text{if } 1 \leq r \leq c
    \end{cases}
$$

**Inclusion probabilities**

$$\pi_i=\text{Prob}(i\in s)=1/G$$

$$
  \pi_{ij} =
    \begin{cases}
      1/G & \text{if } i, j \text{ belong to the same sample}\\
      0 & \text{otherwise}
    \end{cases}
$$

## Selection method

- the systematic design is NOT measurable
- there is no unbiased estimator of the variance

# The HT Estimator

## Important

The systematic design can be viewed as selecting a single cluster (group) out of the $G$ possible ones.

To select the sample, the population $U$ is partitioned into $G$ clusters:

$$U = U_1\cup U_2\cup\dots\cup U_G $$
$$N=\sum\limits_{r=1}^G N_r $$

The total of variable $y$ can be written as:

$$Y=\sum\limits_{i\in U}y_i=\sum\limits_{r=1}^G\sum\limits_{i\in U_r}y_i=\sum\limits_{r=1}^G t_r$$

## HT estimator

The HT estimator for $Y$ is:

$$\hat Y_{\text{HT}}=G\left(\sum\limits_{i\in U_r}y_i\right)=G\times t_r$$

The variance of the estimator $\hat Y_{\text{HT}}$ is:

$$V_{SY}(\hat Y_{\text{HT}})=G^2(1-1/G)\,\text{var}[t_r] =G\sum\limits_{r=1}^G(t_r-\bar t)^2$$

where $\text{var}[t_r]=(G-1)^{-1}\sum\limits_{r=1}^G(t_r-\bar t)^2$ with $\bar t=\sum\limits_{r=1}^G t_r/G$.

## Systematic variance

If we assume that $N=nG$:

$$V(\hat Y_{\text{HT}})=G\sum\limits_{r=1}^G(t_r-\bar t)^2=Gn^2\sum\limits_{r=1}^G(\bar y_r-\bar y_U)^2$$

We can decompose the variability using ANOVA:

$$\sum\limits_{i \in U}(y_i-\bar y_U)^2=\sum\limits_{r=1}^G\sum\limits_{i\in U_r}(y_i-\bar y_r)^2+n\sum\limits_{r=1}^G(\bar y_r-\bar y_U)^2$$

$$SST=SSW+SSB$$

For the design to be "efficient", the samples must be similar to each other and very heterogeneous "within".

$$V_{SY}=Gn\,(SSB) $$

## Intra-sample heterogeneity coefficient

$$\delta = 1 - \left[\frac{N-1}{N-G}\frac{SSW}{SST}\right]$$

- If $SSW=0$ (worst case), $\delta=1$ (maximum value).
- If $SSB=0$ then $SST=SSW$, $\delta=-\left[\frac{G-1}{N-G}\right]$ (minimum value).

## Design effect

Under a systematic design (SY) where $N=Gn$:

$$V_{SY}=\frac{N^2\,\text{var}_U[y]}{n}\left[(1-f)+(n-1)\delta\right] $$

Then,

$$\text{deff}(SY,\hat Y_{\text{HT}})=1+\frac{n-1}{1-f}\delta $$

the systematic design is more efficient if $\delta<0$ (i.e. $SSW>SST$).
